---
title: "The method"
---

System identification here is an iterative, information-optimal loop.
The key insight is that **measurement time on a real interferometer is expensive**,
and drive amplitude is bounded — so you must spend both wisely.
Rather than sweeping uniformly across frequency and hoping for the best,
`system_ident` solves the inverse problem: *given a prior model and a fixed
drive-power budget, where should the excitation energy go to extract the most
information about the model parameters?*

The answer comes from Fisher information theory.

## The loop

```
   prior model ──► design optimal excitation ──► inject (Tukey-ramped) ──► measure
        ▲                                                                      │
        └────────── re-fit model (invfreqs) ◄─── accumulate (inv-var weight) ◄┘
```

::: {.callout-note}
## One sentence

Given a prior model, `system_ident` computes exactly how much each frequency
contributes to parameter information, puts the drive energy there, measures,
re-fits, and repeats — converging to parameter uncertainties far below what
equal-power flat excitation can achieve.
:::

Each iteration does four things:

1. **Design** — compute the dispersion function ν(f) from the current model,
   readout noise ASD, and drive budget; run the Pintelon–Schoukens fixed-point
   iteration to obtain the optimal excitation ASD.

2. **Inject** — synthesise a time series from the ASD (random-phase, Tukey-ramped),
   send it through the backend (twin or CDS hardware), and record the response.

3. **Accumulate** — inverse-variance-weight the new transfer-function estimate
   with all previous ones, frequency bin by frequency bin.  The first pass uses
   a flat broadband excitation for global conditioning; the accumulated estimate
   carries that broadband coverage forward permanently.

4. **Re-fit** — run `InvfreqsEstimator` on the accumulated TF estimate to update
   the model; check the fractional-uncertainty stop criterion.

## Why Fisher information?

The Fisher information matrix `I(θ)` bounds how precisely any unbiased estimator
can recover parameters θ from data. Its inverse `I(θ)⁻¹` is the Cramér–Rao lower
bound on parameter covariance. For a linear system driven by a stationary input
with PSD `Pxx(f)` and measured in readout noise with PSD `Pyy(f)`:

$$
I_{ij}(\theta) \propto T \int \frac{P_{xx}(f)}{P_{yy}(f)} \frac{\partial G^*(f)}{\partial \theta_i} \frac{\partial G(f)}{\partial \theta_j} \, df
$$

The optimal `Pxx(f)` maximises `log det I(θ)` — the log volume of the uncertainty
ellipsoid — subject to ∫ Pxx(f) df = constant (fixed power budget).  This leads to
a closed-form water-filling condition whose fixed point is the dispersion-weighted
allocation in `design.pintelon`.

## Why iterative?

The optimal excitation depends on the current model through the Jacobian ∂G/∂θ
and the dispersion function. As the model improves pass by pass, so does the
excitation design — the loop progressively sharpens its focus toward the
frequencies that are most informative *given what it has already learned*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The first pass is special

`SysIDLoop` always runs pass 1 with a flat, broadband excitation.
This ensures the global transfer function is well-sampled before the optimal
designer concentrates power on specific features — preventing the model from
converging to a local minimum caused by poor initial coverage.
:::

## References

Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*,
2nd ed., IEEE Press / Wiley, 2012 — §5.4.2 (optimal excitation design),
§7 (weighted least-squares estimation).

[LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher expressions for
suspension parameters.

[LIGO-G1400084](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G1400084) (Larry Price) — original
motivation and prior work.
